notes: Accrington is a mill town in the Hyndburn borough of Lancashire, on the edge of the Pennines. It grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution around cotton spinning and weaving, and later became famous for the distinctive hard, dense "Accrington NORI" bricks used in the foundations of the Empire State Building and Blackpool Tower. The town's name is inseparable from the football club Accrington Stanley, one of the twelve founder members of the Football League in 1888 (the original club folded in 1962, and a phoenix club later revived the name, eventually returning to the Football League in 2006). Accrington's economy today rests on light manufacturing, retail and services, having diversified away from its declining textile base through the 20th century. The surrounding countryside includes reservoirs and moorland popular with walkers, and the town retains Victorian civic architecture including its market hall and town hall reflecting its industrial-era prosperity.

Aldershot in Hampshire is known as the "Home of the British Army," having hosted a huge permanent garrison since Aldershot Camp was established in 1854 as a training base. Military heritage still dominates the town's identity, economy and skyline, with barracks, parade grounds and army museums alongside a large civilian population. Aldershot Town F.C. ("the Shots") plays at the Recreation Ground; the original Aldershot F.C. was a Football League founder-era club that folded in 1992, and Aldershot Town was formed the same year, later reaching the Football League itself. The town forms part of the Rushmoor borough alongside neighbouring Farnborough, whose combined population passed 100,000 at the 2021 census. Beyond the military, Aldershot's economy includes retail, logistics and light industry, and it sits within commuting distance of London along the M3 corridor.

Altrincham is an affluent market town in the Metropolitan Borough of Trafford, Greater Manchester, granted its market charter in 1290, making it one of England's oldest boroughs. It thrived as a Victorian and Edwardian commuter suburb after the railway arrived in 1849, and its centre has been revitalised in recent years around an award-winning indoor food market and independent retail scene, earning a reputation as one of the "coolest" towns in the north of England. Altrincham F.C. plays in non-league football at Moss Lane and reached national attention with FA Cup and Conference title success in the 1980s. The town's economy blends professional services, retail and hospitality, and it borders the genteel suburbs of Hale and Bowdon, contributing to its reputation for high living standards within the Manchester conurbation.

Barnsley in South Yorkshire grew from a medieval market town into a major coal-mining and glass-manufacturing centre during the Industrial Revolution, at one time surrounded by dozens of collieries and linen-weaving works. The town's identity was profoundly shaped by mining, including the 1866 Oaks Colliery disaster, one of Britain's worst, and by the 1984-85 miners' strike after pit closures began. Post-industrial regeneration has focused on retail, digital and public-sector employment, alongside the landmark Glass Works development in the town centre. Barnsley F.C., "the Tykes," play at Oakwell and reached the FA Cup final in 1910 and 1912. The wider Metropolitan Borough of Barnsley had a 2021 census population of about 244,600. The town retains a strong sense of Yorkshire working-class identity and hosts the Barnsley Civic arts venue.

Barrow-in-Furness is a shipbuilding town on the Furness peninsula in Cumbria, transformed in the mid-19th century from a small hamlet into one of the world's great shipbuilding and steelmaking centres after iron ore deposits were found nearby and the Furness Railway and docks were built. BAE Systems' Barrow shipyard, one of the largest in Europe, has built Royal Navy submarines including the Vanguard and Astute classes and continues to dominate the local economy. The town has nearby Furness Abbey, an important medieval Cistercian ruin, and Piel Island with its castle. Barrow A.F.C., nicknamed "the Bluebirds," play at Holker Street and returned to the Football League in 2020 after decades in non-league football. The 2021 census recorded a population decline from 2011, reflecting long-term economic restructuring.

Birkenhead sits on the Wirral peninsula across the River Mersey from Liverpool, connected by the Mersey Tunnels and historic ferries. It grew explosively in the 19th century around William Laird's shipyard (later Cammell Laird), which built the first British-built ironclad warship and remains a major shipbuilding and engineering employer. Birkenhead Park, opened in 1847, was the world's first publicly funded civic park and directly inspired the design of New York's Central Park. Tranmere Rovers F.C. play at Prenton Park and have a long non-league and Football League history including notable FA Cup giant-killings. The town's economy today combines maritime engineering, logistics and retail, and it retains substantial Victorian architecture alongside regeneration projects along its historic dock waterfront.

Birmingham is England's second-largest city, the industrial powerhouse of the West Midlands and a driving force of the Industrial Revolution, earning the nickname "the city of a thousand trades" for its extraordinary diversity of metalworking, jewellery-making and manufacturing. Its canal network exceeds Venice's in length, a legacy of its role as a manufacturing and transport hub. Birmingham hosted the 2022 Commonwealth Games and is a major centre for finance, law, education (University of Birmingham, Aston University) and the arts, including the Birmingham Royal Ballet and City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra. It is a highly diverse, youthful city with a large South Asian and Caribbean heritage population. Football looms large: Birmingham City and Aston Villa (a founding member of the Football League in 1888) are both based here, giving the city one of England's fiercest local derbies.

Blackburn, in Lancashire, was one of the archetypal cotton-weaving towns of the Industrial Revolution, home to James Hargreaves who invented the spinning jenny there around 1764. At its peak Blackburn was the world's largest producer of cotton cloth, and its mill chimneys and Victorian civic buildings, including the striking Blackburn Cathedral, still mark the townscape. The town, immortalised in the Beatles lyric "four thousand holes in Blackburn, Lancashire" from "A Day in the Life," today forms the unitary authority of Blackburn with Darwen. Blackburn Rovers, another 1888 Football League founder member, won the Premier League title in 1995 under Jack Walker's ownership and play at Ewood Park. The local economy has diversified into engineering, food processing and services following the decline of textiles.

Blackpool is Britain's classic seaside resort, rising to prominence in the Victorian era as textile workers from Lancashire's mill towns flocked there by rail for their "wakes weeks" holidays. Its skyline is defined by Blackpool Tower (1894, inspired by the Eiffel Tower), the Pleasure Beach amusement park, and the illuminated Golden Mile promenade, with the annual Blackpool Illuminations lighting display running each autumn. The town remains a major centre for the amusement, hospitality and tourism industries, alongside a growing conference trade, though it has faced significant socio-economic challenges in recent decades. Blackpool F.C., "the Tangerines," play at Bloomfield Road and won the FA Cup in 1953 in the famous "Matthews Final" featuring Stanley Matthews, and were promoted to the Premier League in 2010.

Bolton, in Greater Manchester, was a major cotton-spinning town during the Industrial Revolution, home to inventor Samuel Crompton, who developed the spinning mule there in 1779, a machine that transformed textile manufacturing worldwide. Its grand Victorian town hall and the Bolton Museum reflect the wealth generated by textiles and engineering in that era. Today the town's economy is centred on retail, healthcare, education and light manufacturing, following the decline of the mills through the 20th century. Bolton Wanderers, one of the twelve founding members of the Football League in 1888, won the FA Cup four times, including the first Wembley final in 1923 (the "White Horse Final"), and now play at the University of Bolton Stadium after decades at Burnden Park. The town lies at the foot of the West Pennine Moors.

Borehamwood, in Hertfordshire just north of London, is renowned as a centre of the British film and television industry, home to Elstree Studios (long associated with Borehamwood) where classics including several Star Wars films, The Shining and long-running soap opera EastEnders have been produced. The town grew rapidly in the 20th century from a small hamlet into a substantial commuter and media-industry settlement, benefiting from its rail links into London. Borehamwood F.C. plays non-league football, but the town is more widely known through its studios than through sport. Its economy today blends the creative and media sector with retail, logistics and commuting residents who work in London, and it forms part of the Hertsmere borough alongside historic Elstree village.

Boston is a historic market town and port in Lincolnshire on the River Witham, whose name was given to Boston, Massachusetts, by Puritan emigrants who left from the area in the 1630s, including passengers connected to the Mayflower voyage. Its landmark is St Botolph's Church, known as "the Stump," whose tower has guided sailors and travellers across the flat Lincolnshire fens for centuries. The town's economy has long depended on agriculture and food processing thanks to the fertile surrounding farmland, and more recently on logistics tied to its port. Boston United F.C., "the Pilgrims," play at the Jakemans Stadium and have a strong non-league pedigree including FA Trophy wins. The wider Borough of Boston had a 2021 census population of about 70,500, reflecting significant growth from immigration into the agricultural workforce.

Bournemouth is a South Coast seaside resort in Dorset, purpose-built as a genteel Victorian spa and holiday town from the 1810s onward around pine-scented "chines" (wooded ravines) leading to seven miles of sandy beach. It became a major tourism destination and later a centre for the financial services and insurance sector as well as language schools and two universities, Bournemouth University and Arts University Bournemouth. Since 2019 it has formed part of the unitary authority of Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole. AFC Bournemouth, "the Cherries," play at the Vitality Stadium and reached the Premier League for the first time in 2015 under manager Eddie Howe after a dramatic rise from the lower leagues. The town hosts a well-known annual air festival on its seafront.

Bradford in West Yorkshire was one of the great Victorian "Worstedopolis" wool-textile towns, its mills and warehouses, including the landmark Lister's Mill, built on wealth from worsted cloth manufacture and German-Jewish merchant families who settled there. The city's Saltaire model village, built by mill owner Titus Salt, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site nearby. Bradford has one of England's largest South Asian communities, reflecting mid-20th-century immigration to work in the textile mills, giving it a distinctive multicultural character celebrated through its curry houses and the National Science and Media Museum. Bradford City won the FA Cup in 1911 and endured the tragic 1985 Valley Parade fire, a disaster that transformed UK stadium safety regulation. Bradford was UK City of Culture for 2025, marking a major regeneration push.

Brighton and Hove, on England's South Coast in East Sussex, grew from a fishing village into Britain's most fashionable Georgian and Regency seaside resort after the Prince Regent (later George IV) built the exotic Royal Pavilion there in the early 19th century, popularising sea-bathing among the elite. The twin towns, unified as a single city in 2000, are known today for a famously liberal, bohemian and LGBTQ-friendly culture, a large annual Pride festival, the Brighton Festival arts event, and a thriving university sector around the University of Sussex and University of Brighton. The seafront's Brighton Palace Pier and now-ruined West Pier are iconic landmarks. Brighton & Hove Albion, "the Seagulls," moved from the Goldstone Ground to the Amex Stadium in 2011 and established themselves as a stable Premier League club through astute recruitment and European qualification in 2023.

Bristol is a historic port city in South West England that grew wealthy from Atlantic trade from the medieval period onward, including, controversially, its central role in the transatlantic slave trade, a history now publicly confronted following the 2020 toppling of the Edward Colston statue. Its maritime heritage includes Brunel's SS Great Britain and Clifton Suspension Bridge, both enduring symbols of the city's 19th-century engineering prowess. Bristol today is a hub for aerospace engineering (Airbus, Rolls-Royce), creative media (home to the BBC's Natural History Unit and Aardman Animations), and a vibrant street-art scene associated with Bristol-born artist Banksy. The city fields two Football League clubs, Bristol City and Bristol Rovers, contesting a long-running local derby. Bristol was the fastest-growing of England's "Core Cities" in the decade to the 2021 census.

Bromley is a large outer-London borough in Kent's historic hinterland, retaining a more suburban, leafy character than inner London and containing significant green belt land, including parts of the North Downs. The town of Bromley itself grew as a market town and later a Victorian railway commuter suburb; it was the birthplace of author H. G. Wells in 1866. The borough's economy is largely residential and service-based, with a busy town-centre shopping district and significant commuting into central London. Bromley F.C., nicknamed "the Ravens," play at Hayes Lane and were promoted to the Football League for the first time in 2024 after winning the National League. The London Borough of Bromley, formed in 1965, is geographically the largest of the 32 London boroughs.

Burnley is a former cotton-weaving town in Lancashire that was, by the late 19th century, the world's largest producer of cotton cloth, its economy built around hundreds of weaving sheds powered by nearby coal. The Weavers' Triangle area preserves mills, canal wharves and workers' housing from this era along the Leeds and Liverpool Canal. Following deindustrialisation, the town's economy has diversified into aerospace components, food manufacturing and advanced engineering. Burnley F.C., "the Clarets," won the Football League title in 1960 and the FA Cup in 1914, and play at Turf Moor, one of the oldest continuously used grounds in English football; the club has moved between the Premier League and Championship repeatedly in recent seasons. The surrounding South Pennine moorland and Pendle Hill give the area strong associations with the Lancashire witch trials of 1612.

Burslem is one of the six towns that federated in 1910 to form the city of Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, and is often called the "Mother Town" of the Potteries as the district where the region's pottery industry first flourished. It was the birthplace of Josiah Wedgwood in 1730, whose ceramics works helped establish Stoke-on-Trent's global reputation for fine china and earthenware, and many bottle-kiln era pottery buildings survive in the town. Burslem's population and economy declined sharply through the 20th century as the pottery industry contracted, though heritage regeneration schemes have targeted its historic Market Place and Wedgwood Institute. Port Vale F.C., "the Valiants," have played in Burslem since 1884 and are based at Vale Park, giving the small town an outsized footballing profile relative to its modest population at the 2021 census.

Burton upon Trent, in Staffordshire, is world-famous as the historic capital of English brewing, its mineral-rich water (high in gypsum, giving rise to the process known as "Burtonisation") having made it ideal for pale ale production since the 18th century. Breweries including Bass, Ind Coope and Marston's built the town's Victorian prosperity, and while consolidation has reduced the number of breweries, Burton remains home to major brewing operations and the National Brewery Centre museum. The town's economy has diversified into logistics and food manufacturing, benefiting from its central England location near the A38 and A50. Burton Albion F.C. reached the Football League for the first time in 2009 and play at the Pirelli Stadium, adding a modern footballing chapter to a town whose identity has for centuries been inseparable from beer.

Cambridge is a historic university city in the East of England, home to the University of Cambridge, founded in 1209 and one of the world's oldest and most prestigious universities, whose historic colleges, chapels (notably King's College Chapel) and the River Cam, popular for punting, define the city's character. Cambridge has become a global hub for technology and biotechnology, dubbed "Silicon Fen," hosting major research campuses and start-ups spun out of the university in fields from AI to genomics. The city had the fastest population growth of any district in the East of England in the decade to the 2021 census. Cambridge United F.C. play in the lower reaches of the Football League at the Abbey Stadium, a comparatively modest footballing presence in a city better known worldwide for academia and innovation.

Cardiff is the capital of Wales, having only formally gained that status in 1955, and grew from a small town into one of the world's busiest coal-exporting ports during the 19th century, funnelling coal from the South Wales valleys through Cardiff Bay's docks built by the Marquesses of Bute. Much of that dockland was transformed through late-20th-century regeneration into the Cardiff Bay waterfront, now home to the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) and Wales Millennium Centre. The city centre's Cardiff Castle sits on Roman foundations, reflecting nearly two thousand years of continuous settlement. Cardiff hosts the Principality Stadium, a national venue for rugby and football finals, while Cardiff City F.C., "the Bluebirds," play at Cardiff City Stadium and won the FA Cup in 1927, the only time it has left England. Cardiff was Wales' fastest-growing local authority in the decade to the 2021 census.

Carlisle is a border city in Cumbria with a history stretching back to the Roman fort of Luguvalium, near the western end of Hadrian's Wall, and it endured centuries of Anglo-Scottish border warfare as a heavily fortified garrison city, reflected in Carlisle Castle's turbulent history. Its cathedral, one of England's smallest, dates from the 12th century. Carlisle grew as a railway and textile hub in the Victorian era (notably biscuit manufacturer Carr's, founded there in 1831) and remains an important rail junction and regional service centre for a large, sparsely populated rural hinterland in Cumbria. Carlisle United F.C., "the Cumbrians," play at Brunton Park, England's most northerly Football League ground, and are one of the more geographically isolated clubs in the English game, with no other league club within roughly forty miles.

Cheltenham is a Regency spa town in Gloucestershire that rose to prominence after mineral springs were discovered in 1716, drawing fashionable visitors including King George III in 1788, whose royal visit cemented the town's status as England's most complete Regency townscape, with elegant terraces, crescents and the tree-lined Promenade. The town is world-famous for the Cheltenham Festival, the pinnacle of National Hunt horse racing, held each March at Cheltenham Racecourse, and also hosts major literature, science and jazz festivals. Its economy today combines tourism, education (Cheltenham Ladies' College and Cheltenham College) and a significant technology and cyber-security sector centred on the nearby GCHQ intelligence agency. Cheltenham Town F.C., "the Robins," play at Whaddon Road and have spent periods in League One and League Two in recent decades.

Chesterfield, in Derbyshire on the edge of the Peak District, is instantly recognisable for the twisted and leaning spire of its parish church, St Mary and All Saints, known as the "Crooked Spire," reputedly warped through a combination of medieval timber-seasoning error and lead cladding weight. The town developed as a market and later an industrial centre for coal mining, iron founding and engineering, with links to railway pioneer George Stephenson, who lived near Chesterfield and is buried at Holy Trinity Church. Its economy today rests on retail, engineering and logistics, aided by proximity to the M1 motorway. Chesterfield F.C., "the Spireites," play at the SMH Group Stadium and returned to the Football League in 2024 after winning the National League, reconnecting the town with league football after a period outside it.

Colchester in Essex claims to be Britain's oldest recorded town, known to the Romans as Camulodunum and briefly the capital of Roman Britain before Londinium, a heritage visible in its Roman walls, the Balkerne Gate and Colchester Castle, built atop the razed Temple of Claudius after Boudica's revolt burned the town in AD 60/61. Colchester was granted city status in 2022 as part of the Queen's Platinum Jubilee honours, formalising a status many felt its history already merited. The town's economy blends its role as a garrison town for the British Army, retail and services, university education through the University of Essex, and surrounding agriculture. Colchester United F.C., "the U's," play at the JobServe Community Stadium and have historically been known as a lower-league club with occasional cup-upset pedigree.

Coventry is a cathedral city in the West Midlands that was one of England's largest and wealthiest medieval cities, famous for Coventry blue cloth and Lady Godiva's legendary ride. It became a major bicycle- and later car-manufacturing centre (Jaguar, Rover, Triumph) before much of its historic core was destroyed in the devastating November 1940 Luftwaffe bombing raid. The rebuilt city centre features Basil Spence's modernist Coventry Cathedral (1962) beside the ruins of the old cathedral, and Europe's first pedestrianised shopping precinct. Coventry was UK City of Culture in 2021 and was the birthplace of the 2 Tone ska movement (The Specials). It is home to Coventry City F.C., who play at the CBS Arena.

Crawley began as a small Saxon market town on the London-to-Brighton road and grew through the medieval and coaching-inn era. Its modern character was shaped after 1947, when it was designated one of Britain's post-war New Towns, triggering rapid planned expansion into 14 residential neighbourhoods around the historic centre. Today Crawley's economy is dominated by services tied to neighbouring Gatwick Airport, along with retail, logistics and pharmaceuticals. The town is notably diverse, home to a large Chagossian community, and hosts the long-running World Marbles Championship at nearby Tinsley Green. Its football club, Crawley Town F.C., plays in the English Football League at the Broadfield Stadium.

Crewe is a Cheshire town that owes its existence to the railway: it grew from a rural hamlet into a major junction and engineering centre after the Grand Junction Railway opened a station there in 1837, with the London and North Western Railway's works once employing over 20,000 people. Crewe remains an important rail junction today and is also home to Bentley Motors' car factory, a major local employer. Cultural landmarks include the Lyceum Theatre, Queen's Park and the Crewe Heritage Centre, celebrating the town's railway heritage. Its football club, Crewe Alexandra, founded in 1877 by railway workers, is known for developing young talent through its academy under long-serving manager Dario Gradi.

Derby is a cathedral city in Derbyshire with origins as the Roman settlement of Derventio, later becoming an important centre of the early Industrial Revolution, including one of the world's first factories, Lombe's silk mill. It grew into a major railway manufacturing hub as headquarters of the Midland Railway, and remains a centre of advanced engineering today, anchored by Rolls-Royce (aero engines) and Toyota's UK car plant. Derby gained city status in 1977 and possesses a cathedral dating from 1927. The city has a significant deaf community and a growing video-game development sector. Its football club, Derby County F.C. ('the Rams'), plays at Pride Park Stadium.

Doncaster began as the Roman fort of Danum and grew into a prosperous medieval market town before booming during the railway age, when its Plant Works built famous locomotives including the Flying Scotsman and Mallard. Known for its racing and railway heritage, the city hosts the historic Doncaster Racecourse (home of the St Leger, the oldest classic horse race) alongside modern logistics operations including Doncaster Sheffield Airport and a major rail freight interchange. Cultural attractions include Doncaster Museum, the CAST theatre and nearby Yorkshire Wildlife Park. The city's football club, Doncaster Rovers, plays at the Eco-Power Stadium.

Eastleigh is a Hampshire town on the River Itchen that grew from small villages into a substantial settlement after the London and South Western Railway established locomotive works there around 1890-1900; the town was named by novelist Charlotte Yonge, who helped fund its parish church. The Supermarine Spitfire made its maiden flight from Eastleigh Aerodrome in 1936, a source of local pride. The economy today centres on retail, logistics and manufacturing, with employers including B&Q's head office and Prysmian Cables. Comedian Benny Hill was a notable former resident. Eastleigh F.C. ('the Spitfires') represent the town in the National League.

notes: Edgware is a suburban district straddling the London boroughs of Barnet and Harrow, its name deriving from Old English for 'Ecgi's weir'. Long a rural Middlesex parish, it was transformed after the Northern line reached it in 1924, rapidly urbanising into a commuter suburb with the Broadwalk shopping centre at its heart. Edgware is notable for its ethnic and religious diversity, including one of London's largest Jewish communities alongside sizeable Hindu and Muslim populations. Its economy shifted over the 20th century from gravel extraction and light manufacturing to retail and services. Edgware Town F.C. is the area's local football club.

Exeter is the cathedral city and county town of Devon, founded as the Roman fort of Isca around AD 55 and later a Saxon stronghold that withstood Viking raids. It flourished in the medieval and early modern period as a major wool-trading centre, and its cathedral boasts the longest continuous medieval stone vault in the world. Heavily damaged during World War II's 'Baedeker Blitz', much of the centre was rebuilt afterwards. Today Exeter is a hub for education, business and tourism in the South West, home to the University of Exeter, the Met Office headquarters, and UNESCO City of Literature status. Its football club, Exeter City F.C., plays at St James Park.

Fleetwood is a purpose-built Lancashire seaside and fishing town founded in the 1830s by landowner Peter Hesketh-Fleetwood and laid out by architect Decimus Burton, whose two lighthouses from 1840 still stand. It grew into one of Britain's major fishing ports through the 20th century until the Cod Wars with Iceland devastated the industry in the 1960s-70s. Today its best-known product is Fisherman's Friend lozenges, made locally by Lofthouse of Fleetwood and exported worldwide. The town retains a Victorian market and hosts the Fylde Folk Festival. Fleetwood Town F.C., nicknamed 'the Cod Army', reached the Football League in 2012.

Gateshead sits on the south bank of the Tyne opposite Newcastle, with roots recorded by the Venerable Bede in the 7th century. It grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution around coal mining, iron and shipbuilding, then faced sharp decline in the later 20th century. Regeneration has since made Gateshead a cultural landmark, home to the Angel of the North sculpture, the Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art, the Sage Gateshead music venue and the Millennium Bridge. Its football club, Gateshead F.C., plays in the National League after a controversial vote removed the club from the Football League in 1960.

Gillingham developed from a small settlement near Chatham Dockyard into a substantial town as Royal Navy activity expanded through the 19th century, though the dockyard's 1984 closure brought economic upheaval. It now forms part of the Medway unitary authority alongside Chatham and Rochester, with an economy built on retail, business parks and services. Landmarks include the Royal Engineers Museum and St Mary Magdalene church, and regeneration schemes continue to revive the High Street. Gillingham F.C., founded in 1893 and based at Priestfield Stadium ('the Gills'), reached the second tier of English football in 2000.

Grimsby, on the Lincolnshire coast at the mouth of the Humber, traces its origins to a Viking settlement traditionally founded by a fisherman named Grim. Dock improvements from the late 18th century sparked rapid growth, and by the 1950s it was the world's largest fishing port. The industry collapsed after the 1970s Cod Wars with Iceland and the loss of distant-water fishing rights, but Grimsby has reinvented itself as a food-processing centre, branded 'Europe's Food Town', hosting hundreds of food companies. Landmarks include Grimsby Minster and the Fishing Heritage Centre. Its football club, Grimsby Town F.C. ('the Mariners'), plays at Blundell Park.

Halifax is a West Yorkshire mill town whose wealth was built on the wool trade from medieval times, symbolised by the grand 18th-century Piece Hall cloth market. It became notorious for the Halifax Gibbet, an early guillotine used on thieves until 1650. During the Industrial Revolution it grew into a major textile and carpet manufacturing centre, and later became known for confectionery (Mackintosh's Quality Street and Rolo) and as home to the Halifax Building Society/bank. Cultural attractions include Halifax Minster, the restored Piece Hall and the Eureka! children's museum. FC Halifax Town competes in the National League.

Harrogate is a North Yorkshire spa town that grew from two 16th-century settlements around mineral springs discovered in the Tudor period, earning it the nickname 'the English Spa' as fashionable visitors flocked to take the waters during the Georgian and Victorian eras. It remains a prosperous, well-preserved town known for its parks and gardens, including the RHS garden at Harlow Carr, and has become a major conference and exhibition destination, home to Harrogate Convention Centre and tea merchant Taylors of Harrogate. The town hosts arts festivals and antiques fairs. Harrogate Town A.F.C. earned promotion to the English Football League via the National League play-offs in 2020.

Hartlepool is a County Durham port town with origins in a 7th-century Anglo-Saxon monastery on its headland. It expanded dramatically in the 19th century when West Hartlepool was built as a coal-exporting dock town, later merging with the old town in 1967. Its economy has long depended on maritime trades, engineering, chemicals and the nearby Hartlepool nuclear power station. The town is famous for the legend that locals hanged a monkey mistaken for a French spy during the Napoleonic Wars, giving fans the enduring nickname 'Monkey Hangers'. Attractions include the National Museum of the Royal Navy and Tall Ships events. Hartlepool United play in the National League.

High Wycombe is a Buckinghamshire market town on the London-to-Oxford route that became the country's leading centre of furniture-making, particularly Windsor chairs, producing an estimated 4,700 chairs a day at its 1875 peak. Landmarks include the 1757 Guildhall and nearby Hughenden Manor, former home of Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli. Today the town is a commercial, retail and educational centre, home to Buckinghamshire New University, with its motto 'Industria ditat' ('Industry enriches') reflecting its manufacturing heritage. Wycombe Wanderers F.C., founded in 1887, play at Adams Park.

Huddersfield is a West Yorkshire town that grew from a market settlement into a major Victorian centre of the woollen textile industry, powered by fast-flowing Pennine rivers. Its railway station, with a grand neoclassical facade, was famously called 'the most splendid station facade in England' by poet John Betjeman. The University of Huddersfield is now the town's largest employer, alongside continuing engineering and manufacturing. Huddersfield is regarded as the birthplace of rugby league, founded there in 1895, and hosts a noted contemporary music festival and choral tradition. Huddersfield Town A.F.C., three-time English champions in the 1920s, play at the John Smith's Stadium.

Ipswich, the county town of Suffolk, has been continuously settled since the Anglo-Saxon period, when it was a major trading port comparable to London and York within East Anglia. Its historic waterfront and streets feature landmarks such as Christchurch Mansion, Ipswich Minster (St Mary-le-Tower) and Norman Foster's modern Willis Building. The town's economy, once built on agriculture and maritime trade, now includes significant insurance and financial-services sectors. It hosts numerous museums, galleries and theatres. Ipswich Town F.C., founded in 1878, won the English league title in 1962 and the UEFA Cup in 1981, and returned to the Premier League in the 2020s.

Kidderminster is a Worcestershire market town recorded in the Domesday Book as Chideminstre, whose economy turned from cloth-making to carpet manufacturing from the early 18th century onward, at one point supplying carpets worldwide; the heritage is preserved at the Museum of Carpet, opened in 2012. Landmarks include the parish church of St Mary and All Saints. Notable natives include postal reformer Sir Rowland Hill and Led Zeppelin singer Robert Plant. Kidderminster Harriers F.C., founded in 1886, is best remembered for a strong FA Cup record, including reaching the fifth round as a non-league side in 1994.

Kingston upon Hull, generally known as Hull, was founded around 1160 as the port of Wyke and renamed by Edward I in 1299. It grew into a major trading and fishing port, prominent in the wool trade, whaling and North Sea fishing, and suffered severe bombing damage in World War II, with about 95% of its houses damaged or destroyed. Today the Port of Hull remains a significant cargo hub, alongside growing energy, healthcare and digital sectors. Hull was UK City of Culture in 2017 and has since become a popular film location nicknamed 'Hullywood'. It is the birthplace of poet Philip Larkin and William Wilberforce. Hull City A.F.C. plays association football, sharing the city with rugby league clubs Hull FC and Hull Kingston Rovers.

Leeds is a major city in West Yorkshire built around the River Aire in the Pennines' eastern foothills. It grew from a medieval manorial borough and wool-trading centre into an 18th-19th century mill town known for textiles, flax and engineering, receiving its city charter in 1893. Today Leeds has one of the UK's most diverse economies, ranking as the largest financial and legal centre outside London, with a large retail, digital and creative sector. The city hosts five universities, a large student population, Kirkgate Market, the Royal Armouries Museum, and major music and arts festivals. Leeds United, founded in 1919, is the city's principal football club, playing at Elland Road.

Leicester is one of England's oldest cities, with roots as an Iron Age settlement that became the Roman town of Ratae Corieltauvorum. It flourished in medieval times under the De Montfort and Lancaster families, and King Richard III was buried there after Bosworth in 1485; his remains were rediscovered beneath a car park in 2012 and reinterred in Leicester Cathedral in 2015. The Industrial Revolution made Leicester a centre for hosiery and footwear manufacturing. Post-war immigration, notably from South Asia and Uganda, created one of England's most ethnically diverse cities. Attractions include the National Space Centre, the Cathedral and the Curve theatre. Leicester City F.C.'s shock 2015-16 Premier League title win brought global attention to the city.

Lincoln is a cathedral city in Lincolnshire that began as an Iron Age settlement before becoming the Roman fortress and colonia of Lindum. In medieval times it was one of England's largest and wealthiest cities, prospering from the wool and cloth trade including the famed 'Lincoln green' fabric. Lincoln Cathedral, completed in stages from 1092, was for centuries the tallest building in the world, and stands beside the Norman Lincoln Castle, which holds an original 1215 Magna Carta. The Industrial Revolution brought heavy engineering, and Lincoln firms built the first tanks during the First World War. Today the economy centres on public administration, healthcare, agriculture and tourism, aided by the University of Lincoln's redevelopment of the Brayford Pool waterfront. Lincoln City F.C. plays in the English Football League.

Liverpool is a major port city in Merseyside founded as a borough in 1207 on the River Mersey. It became one of the world's busiest ports in the 18th and 19th centuries, heavily involved in Atlantic trade including the transatlantic slave trade, and was the departure point for millions of emigrants to the Americas. Its maritime waterfront, including the Pier Head's 'Three Graces', is a UNESCO-recognised heritage area. Liverpool is world-famous as the birthplace of the Beatles and has produced more UK number-one hit singles than any other city. Post-industrial decline was followed by major regeneration, cemented by its role as European Capital of Culture in 2008. The city is home to two Premier League clubs, Liverpool F.C. and Everton F.C., among England's most successful and storied football institutions.

London, the capital of England and the United Kingdom, was founded by the Romans around AD 47 as Londinium on the River Thames. It grew through the Middle Ages around the historic City of London and the seat of government at Westminster, survived the Great Fire of 1666, and became the world's largest city and financial centre during the 19th century British Empire. Today Greater London is one of the world's leading global cities, a hub for finance, business, media, fashion, the arts and education, home to landmarks such as the Tower of London, Buckingham Palace, the Houses of Parliament, and world-class museums like the British Museum and Tate Modern. It is exceptionally multicultural, with over 300 languages spoken. London supports numerous professional football clubs, including Arsenal, Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur, West Ham United, Crystal Palace and Fulham, among the most prominent in English football.

Luton is a town in Bedfordshire that traces its origins to a Saxon settlement on the River Lea, recorded from the 8th century. It grew from an agricultural centre into a major hub of the hat-making industry from the 17th century onward, and later became a centre of car manufacturing through Vauxhall Motors, which operated in the town from 1907 to 2002. Notable buildings include the 12th-century St Mary's Church and the Robert Adam-designed Luton Hoo estate. The town is home to London Luton Airport, a major regional aviation hub opened in 1938, and hosts one of Europe's largest one-day carnivals. Luton Town F.C., nicknamed 'the Hatters' after the local hat trade, won the League Cup in 1988 and has played in the Premier League in recent seasons.

Manchester is a major city in North West England that grew from a Roman fort into the world's first industrialised city during the 19th century, driven by explosive growth in cotton spinning and earning it the nickname 'Cottonopolis'. Its industrial-era warehouses and canals, along with grand Victorian buildings such as the Town Hall, still define much of the cityscape. Following post-war industrial decline and the 1996 IRA bombing, Manchester underwent extensive regeneration and is now a major centre for financial services, media (including the BBC's MediaCityUK), technology and higher education. It is renowned worldwide for its music scene, having produced bands such as Joy Division, The Smiths and Oasis. Manchester is home to two of the world's most famous football clubs, Manchester United and Manchester City.

Mansfield is a market town in Nottinghamshire, about 12 miles north of Nottingham, that received its royal market charter in 1227. Medieval kings including King John maintained a residence there, and the town later became an important centre for Quakerism after George Fox lived there in the 17th century. Coal mining dominated the local economy through much of the 20th century before the industry's decline. Landmarks include the Grade I-listed St Peter and St Paul's Church, recorded in the Domesday Book, and the Carnegie-funded former library, now an arts centre. The town centre has undergone recent regeneration, including redevelopment of a former department store. Mansfield Town F.C., nicknamed 'the Stags', plays at the One Call Stadium and was promoted to League One in 2024.

Middlesbrough is a town on the River Tees in North Yorkshire that grew from a farming hamlet of just 25 people in 1801 into a major industrial powerhouse after Joseph Pease established a coal port there in 1829. It became known as 'Ironopolis', producing roughly a third of the UK's pig iron by the 1870s, and later built a large steel, shipbuilding and chemicals industry. The iconic Tees Transporter Bridge, opened in 1911, remains a symbol of the town. Modern Middlesbrough has diversified into higher education (Teesside University), digital industries and the Wilton International chemical complex, alongside cultural institutions such as the Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art. Middlesbrough F.C. plays at the Riverside Stadium, having moved there in 1995 after 92 years at Ayresome Park.

Milton Keynes is a planned city in Buckinghamshire, designated in 1967 to relieve housing pressure on London and built around a distinctive modernist grid-road system of semi-autonomous neighbourhoods. It absorbed older towns including Bletchley, Wolverton and Stony Stratford, and includes Bletchley Park, the celebrated Allied code-breaking centre of the Second World War. About a quarter of the city is parkland and woodland, linked by an extensive network of cycling and pedestrian 'redways'. Cultural landmarks include Europe's first Peace Pagoda (1980) and the Milton Keynes Gallery. Economically it is one of Britain's most productive and fastest-growing areas, hosting major logistics, retail and technology employers. The city's football club, MK Dons, plays at Stadium MK, and the area is also home to Red Bull Racing's Formula One headquarters.

Nailsworth is a small town in the Cotswolds, within Gloucestershire's Stroud District, built along the Nailsworth Stream which historically powered numerous cloth mills and breweries. A branch railway served the town from 1867 to 1947. Today Nailsworth has a revitalised centre of independent restaurants, cafes and specialty shops, a monthly farmers' market, and traditional customs such as town crier announcements. St George's Church, consecrated in 1900, features stained glass by the noted artist Charles Eamer Kempe, and the surrounding Stroud Valleys attract walkers and cyclists. Despite its tiny size, Nailsworth is home to Forest Green Rovers F.C., based at The New Lawn, which became the smallest settlement ever to host an English Football League club after winning promotion via the 2017 National League play-offs and briefly reaching League One.

Newcastle upon Tyne grew from the Roman settlement of Pons Aelius into a fortified medieval town, taking its modern name from the 'New Castle' built by Robert Curthose in 1080. It rose to prominence through a centuries-long monopoly on coal exports via the Tyne, and later became a major centre for shipbuilding and heavy engineering, home to innovations such as Joseph Swan's incandescent light bulb and Charles Parsons' steam turbine. The elegant neoclassical Grainger Town district, developed in the 1830s, defines much of the city centre alongside the iconic Tyne Bridge. Modern Newcastle is known for its vibrant nightlife, food scene, and universities. Newcastle United F.C., playing at St James' Park since 1886, has won four league titles and six FA Cups, and captured the League Cup in 2025, its first major trophy since 1955.

Newport is a city and county borough in south-east Wales on the River Usk, about 12 miles from Cardiff. Settled by the Normans in the 11th century, it grew into a major coal-exporting port during the 19th-century industrial boom. In 1839 it was the site of the Newport Rising, the last large-scale armed insurrection against authority in mainland Britain, when Chartist protesters clashed with troops. Notable landmarks include the Newport Transporter Bridge, one of only a handful of working transporter bridges left in the world, and Tredegar House. Newport was granted city status in 2002 and has since diversified into aerospace, semiconductors and technology along the M4 corridor; the Celtic Manor Resort nearby hosted the 2010 Ryder Cup and 2014 NATO summit. Newport County A.F.C. represents the city in professional football.

Northampton is a large town in the East Midlands with history dating to the Bronze Age. In medieval times it was home to Northampton Castle, a royal residence that hosted numerous parliaments and the 1164 trial of Thomas Becket. The Great Fire of 1675 destroyed much of the town, prompting a substantial rebuilding, after which Northampton became a major centre of footwear and leather manufacturing, a heritage still reflected in local museums. Designated a New Town in 1968, it experienced significant growth and now serves as the administrative centre of West Northamptonshire and a commuter town for London. Notable sites include Delapre Abbey and several historic churches. Northampton Town F.C., nicknamed 'the Cobblers' after the shoemaking trade, plays at Sixfields Stadium.

Norwich is the county town of Norfolk, established as an Anglo-Saxon settlement and, for much of the second millennium, one of England's largest and wealthiest cities after London, its fortune built on the medieval wool and cloth trade. That wealth funded numerous churches, and Norwich still retains more surviving medieval ecclesiastical buildings than any other city in Western Europe north of the Alps. Landmarks include the Norman Norwich Cathedral and Norwich Castle keep, and the city is often described as the most complete medieval city in the UK, with intact city walls and cobbled lanes. It was designated England's first UNESCO City of Literature in 2012. Historic industries included textiles, shoemaking, chocolate-making (Caley's) and insurance, with Norwich Union founded there in 1797. Norwich City F.C., 'the Canaries', takes its nickname and emblem from birds bred by Flemish weavers who settled in the city.

Nottingham is a major city in the East Midlands with recorded history dating to at least 919 AD, when it was captured by Edward the Elder. It rose to fame during the Industrial Revolution as a global centre of lace manufacturing and textiles, and its legendary association with Robin Hood and the Sheriff of Nottingham draws visitors to Nottingham Castle to this day. The city holds UNESCO City of Literature status, reflecting its literary links to Lord Byron and D. H. Lawrence, and today its economy spans retail, creative industries and life sciences. Nottingham was named 'Home of English Sport' in 2015, hosting international cricket, tennis and other events. It is unusual in having two professional football clubs: Notts County, recognised as the world's oldest professional league club, and Nottingham Forest, European Cup winners in 1979 and 1980 under manager Brian Clough.

Oldham is a historic industrial town in Greater Manchester, about seven miles northeast of Manchester city centre. It transformed during the 19th century from moorland settlements into one of the world's foremost centres of cotton spinning, at its 1909 peak spinning more cotton than France and Germany combined across more than 360 mills. The textile industry finally closed in 1998, and the town's economy has since diversified into retail, healthcare, food processing and publishing, with ongoing regeneration of the town centre. Oldham's built environment still reflects its industrial past through red-brick terraces and surviving mill buildings. The town has a substantial and culturally significant South Asian community alongside its traditional working-class population. Oldham Athletic A.F.C., a former Premier League club, represents the town and plays at Boundary Park.

Oxford is a cathedral city in Oxfordshire renowned as home to the University of Oxford, the oldest university in the English-speaking world, with teaching recorded from the 11th century. Granted city status in 1542, Oxford served as King Charles I's de facto capital during the English Civil War from 1642 to 1646. Its architecture spans every era of English building since the late Anglo-Saxon period, including the Radcliffe Camera and Sheldonian Theatre, earning it the nickname 'City of Dreaming Spires'. Beyond academia, Oxford became an industrial centre after William Morris founded his motor car business there in 1910, and car manufacturing continues today at the Cowley plant, now producing the Mini. The city also has strong publishing (Oxford University Press), science and technology sectors, and draws millions of tourists annually. Oxford United F.C. represents the city in professional football.

Peterborough is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, about 74 miles north of London on the River Nene. It began as the Anglo-Saxon monastery of Medeshamstede around AD 655, which developed into the magnificent Peterborough Cathedral, built largely between 1118 and 1375 in the Early English Gothic style. The arrival of the Great Northern Railway in the 19th century turned the market town into an industrial hub, and Peterborough became the UK's leading brick producer for much of the 20th century using local Fletton clay. Designated a New Town in 1967, it saw rapid growth and modern development, including the Queensgate shopping centre and the Fletton Quays waterfront regeneration. The city's economy now centres on financial services, distribution and a large environmental-business cluster. Peterborough United F.C., nicknamed 'the Posh', plays at the Weston Homes Stadium.

Plymouth is a major port city in Devon with settlement dating to the Bronze Age, formally established as a market town in 1439. It played a pivotal role in English maritime history, helping defeat the Spanish Armada in 1588 and serving as the departure point of the Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower in 1620. Heavily bombed during the Second World War's Plymouth Blitz, the city centre was rebuilt to a modernist plan by Sir Patrick Abercrombie, giving Plymouth much of its present-day layout. It remains a major naval city, home to HMNB Devonport, the largest operational naval base in Western Europe, alongside a strong marine and fishing heritage and three universities. Historic sites include the Barbican quarter and Renaissance-era Prysten House. Plymouth Argyle F.C., 'the Pilgrims', plays at Home Park.

Portsmouth is a historic port city in Hampshire built on Portsea Island, founded around 1180 by the merchant Jean Gisors and granted its royal charter in 1194. It became known as the world's greatest naval port during the height of the British Empire and remains home to two-thirds of the Royal Navy's surface fleet at HMNB Portsmouth. The city pioneered naval innovation, including the world's first dry dock in 1496 and the first mass-production line at the Portsmouth Block Mills. Portsmouth Historic Dockyard preserves famous ships including HMS Victory and the Mary Rose, while the modern Spinnaker Tower dominates the waterfront skyline. Despite heavy bombing in the Second World War, the city played a crucial role in the D-Day landings. It is also the birthplace of Charles Dickens and Isambard Kingdom Brunel. Portsmouth F.C., nicknamed 'Pompey' like the city, represents the area in professional football.

Preston is a city on the River Ribble in Lancashire and the county's administrative centre, granted a Guild Merchant charter in 1179 and city status in 2002. It became a major textile manufacturing hub during the Industrial Revolution, growing rapidly through the 19th century before industrial decline in the 20th. Landmarks include St Walburge's Church, with the tallest spire in England on a non-cathedral church, the Harris Museum and the historic Covered Market. The city has links to the 19th-century Temperance Movement and hosted an early Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints mission. Today Preston's economy centres on higher education (the University of Lancashire), aerospace and defence manufacturing through BAE Systems, and retail, with the city named the UK's 'most improved city' in 2018. Preston North End F.C., one of the founding members of the Football League in 1888, is commemorated locally by a statue of legendary player Tom Finney.

Reading is a major commercial and retail centre in the Thames Valley, about 40 miles west of London, with roots in the 12th-century Reading Abbey, founded in 1121 and largely destroyed during Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries. Historically known for the 'three Bs' of beer, bulbs and biscuits (notably Huntley and Palmers), Reading has transformed into a hub for technology, insurance and financial services, hosting major operations for firms such as Microsoft and Oracle, and now attracts more commuters into the town than it sends out. It has literary associations, including Jane Austen's schooling there and Oscar Wilde's imprisonment at Reading Gaol, which inspired his writing. The town hosts the Reading Festival, one of England's largest music festivals since 1971. Reading F.C. represents the town in professional football.

Rochdale's recorded history begins with an entry in the Domesday Book (1086) as "Recedham Manor"; it received a royal charter in 1251. The town grew into a major centre of England's woollen and cotton trade during the Industrial Revolution, and is renowned as the birthplace of the co-operative movement, founded by the Rochdale Pioneers in 1844. Landmarks include the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall and the birthplace of singer Gracie Fields. The town's economy has diversified from textiles into retail, services and light manufacturing. Rochdale AFC, founded in 1907, plays at Spotland Stadium (the Crown Oil Arena). The wider Metropolitan Borough of Rochdale, part of Greater Manchester, recorded a population of 223,773 at the 2021 Census; the town itself had roughly 111,000 residents.

Rotherham is a market town on the River Don in South Yorkshire, with roots as a medieval market centre granted its charter in 1251. It grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution on the strength of coal mining, iron and steel production, and glass manufacturing. Landmarks include the Chapel on the Bridge, one of only four surviving bridge chapels in England, and the Minster of St Mary. Post-industrial decline since the 1980s prompted regeneration efforts, including riverside developments and the revamped town markets. Rotherham United F.C., nicknamed "the Millers," has played English league football since 1925. The Metropolitan Borough of Rotherham recorded a population of 265,800 at the 2021 Census, the 62nd largest local authority population in England and Wales.

Ruislip is a suburban town in the London Borough of Hillingdon, west London, historically part of Middlesex until 1965. Mentioned in the Domesday Book, it remained a small rural settlement centred on St Martin's Church until the Metropolitan Railway arrived in 1904, triggering rapid interwar suburban housebuilding known as "Metro-land." Notable features include Ruislip Lido, a large artificial lake and country park popular for recreation, and the timber-framed Manor Farm buildings. The area is predominantly residential with a traditional high street of independent shops. Local grassroots football is represented by Ruislip Rangers and Ruislip Eagles. Population figures are complicated by 2022 ward boundary changes; the wider Ruislip area had approximately 58,000 residents at the 2011 Census.

Salford, on the west bank of the River Irwell opposite Manchester, has ancient origins recorded in the Domesday Book and received city status in 1926. It became a major industrial centre in the 19th century, its population surging from around 29,000 in 1801 to nearly 90,000 by 1841 as workers arrived for the textile trade; the 1894 opening of the Manchester Ship Canal and Salford Docks (now MediaCityUK) cemented its industrial importance. Today Salford Quays is a regenerated media and business hub, home to BBC and ITV studios and part of the University of Salford campus. Salford City F.C. and rugby league's Salford Red Devils represent the city in professional sport. The City of Salford recorded a population of 269,900 at the 2021 Census, the fastest-growing local authority in the North West over the preceding decade.

Scunthorpe in North Lincolnshire coalesced in the 19th century from several villages after the 1850s discovery of Frodingham ironstone sparked rapid industrial growth; the town's population rocketed from 1,245 in 1851 to over 45,000 by 1941. It became an urban district in 1891 and remains dominated by steelmaking, home to British Steel's Scunthorpe Works, one of the UK's last integrated steel plants and a frequent subject of national debate over the future of British steel production. The town's nickname, "Steel Town," reflects this heritage. Scunthorpe United F.C., nicknamed "the Iron," has played league football since 1950. Lincolnshire's third most populous settlement after Lincoln and Grimsby, Scunthorpe recorded a population of 81,286 at the 2021 Census.

Sheffield, in South Yorkshire, grew around its rivers' water power to become world-famous for steel and cutlery manufacturing from the medieval period onward, giving rise to "Sheffield steel" and stainless steel, invented there by Harry Brearley in 1913. Granted city status in 1893, its population peaked at 577,050 in 1951 before declining through deindustrialisation, then recovering since the 1990s. The city is exceptionally green, with more trees per capita than any other European city and large areas of the Peak District within its boundary. Landmarks include Sheffield Cathedral, the Winter Garden, and the Crucible Theatre, home of the World Snooker Championship. Sheffield United and Sheffield Wednesday, two of England's oldest professional football clubs, both call the city home. Sheffield's population was 556,500 at the 2021 Census.

Shrewsbury, the county town of Shropshire, sits in a loop of the River Severn and has Anglo-Saxon origins, with institutions dating back as far as the 8th century. Shrewsbury Castle and Shrewsbury Abbey were founded in the 1070s-80s by the Norman Earl of Shrewsbury, Roger de Montgomery, and the town's well-preserved medieval street plan and Tudor timber-framed buildings have earned it a reputation as one of England's finest historic towns. It was the birthplace of Charles Darwin. The economy today centres on retail, tourism, food processing and the county's administrative functions. Shrewsbury Town F.C. plays at the New Meadow stadium. The town's parish population was 76,782 at the 2021 Census.

Solihull, in the West Midlands, grew from a medieval market town centred on St Alphege Church into an affluent suburban and commercial centre southeast of Birmingham. It became a municipal borough in 1954 and merged with Meriden district in 1974 to form the present metropolitan borough. Solihull is closely associated with the automotive industry, hosting Jaguar Land Rover's main manufacturing plant, and is home to Birmingham Airport and the NEC exhibition centre within its boundary. The town centre combines a historic core with modern shopping including the Touchwood centre. Solihull Moors F.C. represents the town in non-league football. The town itself had a population of 126,577 at the 2021 Census, while the wider Metropolitan Borough of Solihull recorded 216,240.

Southampton is a major port city on England's south coast, with origins as the Roman settlement of Clausentum and later the Saxon port of Hamwic. It has been a key embarkation point throughout history, including for the Mayflower in 1620 and the ill-fated Titanic in 1912, and remains one of the UK's principal cruise and container ports. The city sustained heavy bombing in the Southampton Blitz of World War II. Today its economy centres on the port, marine engineering, retail and the University of Southampton. Landmarks include the medieval Bargate and the SeaCity Museum. Southampton F.C., "the Saints," plays at St Mary's Stadium. The city recorded a population of 249,000 at the 2021 Census.

Southend-on-Sea developed in the late 18th century as a fashionable seaside resort (the "South End" of Prittlewell) and expanded rapidly with the arrival of the railway in 1856. It boasts Southend Pier, the longest pleasure pier in the world at 1.34 miles, and was granted city status in 2022 in memory of local MP Sir David Amess. The town's economy blends tourism, retail and a growing financial and insurance sector, alongside London Southend Airport. Its seafront, amusements, and traditional English seaside character continue to draw visitors from London and the South East. Southend United F.C., nicknamed "the Shrimpers," represents the city. Southend-on-Sea's population was 180,700 at the 2021 Census.

Stevenage in Hertfordshire has ancient roots as a settlement on the Great North Road, but its modern character was defined in 1946 when it became Britain's first postwar New Town under the New Towns Act, designed to absorb London's overspill population. Planned with segregated pedestrian and vehicle routes and pioneering residential neighbourhoods, it grew from a small market town into a population centre of nearly 90,000. Today Stevenage is a hub for aerospace and satellite manufacturing, hosting Airbus Defence and Space and MBDA, alongside retail and logistics. The medieval Old Town retains a distinct high street separate from the New Town centre. Stevenage F.C. plays in English league football. The town's population was 89,500 at the 2021 Census.

Stockport, at the confluence of the Rivers Tame and Goyt in Greater Manchester, has a long history as a market town, chartered as a borough in the 13th century, and became a major centre of the cotton and hatting industries during the Industrial Revolution; its distinctive Victorian mill chimneys and the enormous 27-arch Stockport Viaduct still dominate the skyline. The town's extensive network of sandstone tunnels, used as air-raid shelters in World War II, are now a visitor attraction. Modern Stockport's economy is diverse, spanning retail, professional services and a recently regenerated town centre. Stockport County F.C. plays at Edgeley Park. The town/built-up area had a population of 117,935, and the wider Metropolitan Borough of Stockport recorded 294,800, at the 2021 Census.

Stoke-on-Trent, formed in 1910 by the federation of six pottery towns (Tunstall, Burslem, Hanley, Stoke, Fenton and Longton), is known worldwide as "The Potteries" for its ceramics industry, which flourished from the 17th century and employed thousands by the 18th century, aided by the 1777 completion of the Trent and Mersey Canal linking it to Liverpool's ports. Josiah Wedgwood founded his famous pottery works here. Though the ceramics trade has contracted sharply since the late 20th century, firms such as Wedgwood, Emma Bridgewater and Steelite International still operate locally, alongside the Gladstone Pottery Museum. The city achieved city status in 1925. Stoke City F.C. plays at the bet365 Stadium. Stoke-on-Trent's population was 258,400 at the 2021 Census.

Sunderland, at the mouth of the River Wear in North East England, grew from early monastic foundations and fishing settlements into a global leader in shipbuilding from the 14th century onward, at its 19th-century peak hosting over 400 shipyards along the Wear and contributing roughly a third of British merchant tonnage. Coal mining, notably at Monkwearmouth Colliery, was similarly important. Both industries declined sharply in the late 20th century, and the city has since diversified into automotive manufacturing (Nissan's large Washington plant) and digital and creative industries. Sunderland gained city status in 1992. Landmarks include Penshaw Monument and the National Glass Centre. Sunderland A.F.C. plays at the Stadium of Light. The city's population was 274,200 at the 2021 Census.

Sutton is a suburban town in outer south London and the administrative centre of the London Borough of Sutton, historically part of Surrey until 1965. It developed from an agricultural village into a Victorian commuter suburb following the arrival of the London and Croydon Railway in the 1840s, and retains a traditional high street shopping centre. The borough today has a strong reputation for its schools and green space, including the historic Nonsuch Park, once the site of Henry VIII's Nonsuch Palace. Sutton United F.C. plays non-league football at Gander Green Lane and gained fame for FA Cup giant-killing runs. Population growth in the borough (10.2% between 2011 and 2021) outpaced the England average. Sutton's population was 209,600 at the 2021 Census.

Swansea, Wales's second city, sits on the sweeping curve of Swansea Bay at the mouth of the River Tawe and grew from a Norman castle settlement into a major copper-smelting centre in the 18th and 19th centuries, earning the nickname "Copperopolis." Heavily bombed during World War II's "Three Nights' Blitz" (1941), the city centre was substantially rebuilt afterward. Swansea achieved city status in 1969 and is closely associated with poet Dylan Thomas, born and raised there. Its economy today rests on services, retail, higher education (Swansea University) and tourism along the Gower Peninsula, Britain's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. Swansea City A.F.C., "the Swans," plays at the Swansea.com Stadium. The city's population was 238,500 at the 2021 Census.

Swindon in Wiltshire was transformed from a small market town of under 2,000 people into a major railway town after the Great Western Railway chose it as the site of its locomotive works in 1840-43, building an entire company town for its workers. The railway works closed in 1986, and Swindon's economy has since diversified into automotive manufacturing, financial services, distribution and technology, aided by its central location on the M4 corridor. The STEAM Museum preserves the town's railway heritage in the former works buildings. Swindon Town F.C. plays at the County Ground. One of the fastest-growing towns in southern England, Swindon recorded a population of 233,400 at the 2021 Census, growth of 11.6% since 2011.

Tamworth, in Staffordshire, was the historic capital of the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Mercia and home to King Offa and King AEthelflaed, "Lady of the Mercians," making it one of England's most historically significant early medieval towns. Tamworth Castle, a Norman motte-and-bailey structure, overlooks the town. The Industrial Revolution brought textile and paper milling powered by the Rivers Tame and Anker, and later light engineering and distribution took hold thanks to the town's position on major road and rail routes. Modern Tamworth is known for the Snowdome indoor ski centre and nearby Drayton Manor theme park. Tamworth F.C. competes in non-league football. The town's population was 78,600 at the 2021 Census.

Upminster is a suburban town in the London Borough of Havering, on the eastern fringe of Greater London, historically part of Essex. Its name derives from Old English for "the large church on high ground," referring to the Church of St Laurence, where 18th-century rector William Derham conducted early experiments accurately calculating the speed of sound. Agriculture and market gardening dominated until the London, Tilbury and Southend Railway arrived in 1885, spurring suburban growth; the area joined Greater London in 1965. Upminster Windmill, a rare surviving Grade II*-listed mill, is a notable local landmark, alongside the Tithe Barn Museum. Musician Ian Dury's 1981 album "Lord Upminster" referenced the town. Upminster's population was 13,348 at the 2021 Census.

Walsall, in the West Midlands' "Black Country," takes its name from Old English/Welsh roots meaning "valley of the Welsh" and was an established market town by the 13th century. The Industrial Revolution transformed it into a manufacturing centre internationally famous for leather goods, saddles, buckles and chains, with the town's leatherworkers once producing royal handbags; this heritage is preserved at the Walsall Leather Museum. The New Art Gallery Walsall, opened 2000, holds works by Van Gogh and Monet, while Walsall Arboretum (1874) remains a major green space. The town transferred from Staffordshire to the new West Midlands county in 1974. Walsall F.C., "the Saddlers," was founded in 1888. The town/built-up area recorded a population of 70,778 at the 2021 Census.

Watford, in Hertfordshire on the edge of Greater London, developed from a small market town on the River Colne into an industrial centre following the Grand Junction Canal (1798) and London and Birmingham Railway (1837), becoming Britain's leading printing town by the 1920s alongside brewing and paper manufacturing. Post-industrial decline was offset by the town's appeal to corporate headquarters, including JD Wetherspoon and Hilton Worldwide, thanks to its proximity to London. Nearby Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden hosts the Harry Potter studio tour. Cassiobury Park, a 190-acre green space along the Grand Union Canal, is a major local amenity. Watford F.C., "the Hornets," plays at Vicarage Road. The borough's population reached 102,246 at the 2021 Census, up 13.2% from 2011.

Wesham is a small town within the civil parish of Medlar-with-Wesham in Lancashire's Fylde district, near Kirkham and Blackpool. A young settlement by English standards, its modern form dates back only around 160 years, developing after railway expansion connected it to the Fylde coast; the name blends Old English and Old Norse elements. Fox's Biscuits has operated its largest factory here since 1957 in the former Wesham Bakery, producing the well-known "Rocky" biscuit brand, and the town has seen recent commercial growth including a business park and a planned toy factory. AFC Fylde relocated to the nearby Mill Farm Sports Village in 2016. The annual Club Day festival features church processions and brass bands each June. Wesham's population was 3,584 at the 2021 Census.

West Bromwich, in the Black Country borough of Sandwell, appears in the Domesday Book of 1086 and grew into a major 19th-century industrial centre for coal mining, brick making, iron and metal trades including nails, springs and guns. The town suffered heavy World War II bombing and a difficult postwar industrial decline, though the New Square shopping development (2013) and The Public arts centre, designed by Will Alsop, have supported recent regeneration. Historic sites include the Grade II-listed West Bromwich Town Hall (1874-75) and the 17th-century Oak House, where John Wesley preached. Sandwell Valley Country Park adjoins an RSPB nature reserve. West Bromwich Albion F.C., founded 1878, is a central pillar of local identity. The town's population was 103,112 at the 2021 Census.

Wigan, in Greater Manchester, traces its origins to the Roman settlement of Coccium and became a chartered medieval borough in 1246. It grew into a major 19th-century mill town and coal-mining centre, memorialised in George Orwell's 1937 book "The Road to Wigan Pier," which took its name from a former canal coal wharf now a heritage attraction. Post-industrial regeneration has brought retail and leisure development, including the Grand Arcade centre, alongside major employers such as Heinz's European food-processing plant. The town produced acts like The Verve and George Formby, and hosted the legendary Northern Soul venue Wigan Casino (1973-81). Wigan Athletic F.C. and Wigan Warriors rugby league club share the Brick Community Stadium. The wider Metropolitan Borough of Wigan recorded a population of 329,300 at the 2021 Census; the town itself had around 107,700 residents in 2011.

Woking in Surrey grew from a sparsely populated rural area into a commuter town after the London and Southampton Railway arrived in 1838, with further expansion spurred by the mid-1860s London Necropolis Company cemetery. It gained borough status in 1974. Notable historic sites include the ruins of Woking Palace, a royal residence of Henry VII and VIII, and the Shah Jahan Mosque (1889), the first purpose-built mosque in the UK. Author H. G. Wells lived in Woking and set scenes of "The War of the Worlds" there. Economically prosperous overall, ranking first in the 2021 UK Vitality Index, the borough nonetheless faced severe council financial difficulties, declaring effective bankruptcy in 2023. Woking F.C. plays in non-league football. The borough's population was 103,900 at the 2021 Census.

Wolverhampton traces its name to 985, when King AEthelred the Unready granted lands at "Heantun" to Lady Wulfrun by royal charter. A medieval wool-trading centre, it industrialised heavily during the Victorian era around coal mining, steel and lock manufacturing, and achieved city status in 2001. The city has one of England's largest Sikh communities, forming around 12% of the population. Cultural landmarks include Wolverhampton Art Gallery (1884) and the Grand Theatre (1894); in 2017 the "Wolves in Wolves" public art trail displayed 30 wolf sculptures citywide. Today's economy spans aerospace engineering, manufacturing and services, alongside the University of Wolverhampton. Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. plays at Molineux Stadium. The city's population was 263,700 at the 2021 Census.

Worthing on the West Sussex coast grew from a small fishing hamlet into a fashionable Georgian seaside resort in the late 18th century, gaining official town status in 1803 and borough status in 1890. The area has much older roots too, including Neolithic flint mines and the Iron Age hillfort of Cissbury Ring, the borough's highest point. Oscar Wilde wrote "The Importance of Being Earnest" in Worthing and named its protagonist after the town. The Art Deco Worthing Pier, rebuilt after storm and fire damage, was named Britain's best pier in 2019. The service sector, particularly financial services, now dominates the local economy alongside tourism. Worthing F.C. plays in non-league football. The borough's population was 111,400 at the 2021 Census.

Wrexham, in north-east Wales, developed from an 8th-century settlement into a major medieval market town and was, by the 17th century, the largest settlement in Wales. It flourished during the Industrial Revolution through coal, lead and iron mining alongside brewing and leather production, before diversifying into high-tech manufacturing, biotechnology and financial services following industrial decline, aided by one of Europe's largest industrial estates. St Giles' Church, one of the Seven Wonders of Wales, and the Racecourse Ground, the world's oldest international football stadium still in use, are notable landmarks. Wrexham achieved city status in 2022. Wrexham A.F.C., owned by actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney, plays at the Racecourse Ground and has drawn global attention through the "Welcome to Wrexham" documentary series. The built-up area's population was 44,785 at the 2021 Census.

Yeovil in Somerset dates to Saxon times, recorded as "Gifle" in an 880 charter, and developed as a medieval market town before becoming internationally known for glove and leather manufacturing during the 19th century. Its aircraft and defence industries made it a Luftwaffe target in World War II, when bombing killed 49 people and destroyed dozens of homes. Today Leonardo Helicopters (the former Westland Aircraft site) remains the town's principal employer, alongside Honeywell Aerospace. Thomas Hardy fictionalised the town as "Ivell" in his Wessex novels. The 14th-century Church of St John the Baptist and Yeovil Country Park with Ninesprings are notable local features. Yeovil Town F.C. competes in the National League. The built-up area's population was 50,170 at the 2021 Census (parish population 31,633).

York, founded as the Roman fortress and colony of Eboracum in AD 71, later served as the Viking kingdom of Jorvik before becoming a major medieval ecclesiastical and wool-trading centre. The city is renowned for its intact medieval walls, the Gothic York Minster (seat of the Archbishop of York), Clifford's Tower, and the historic Shambles street. The Industrial Revolution brought railways -- York was a major railway hub -- and confectionery manufacturing (Rowntree's and Terry's). Heavily damaged in a 1942 "Baedeker" air raid, the city was extensively restored. Tourism and heritage now anchor the economy, worth over £765 million annually, alongside the University of York (founded 1963) and the National Railway Museum. York's population was 202,800 at the 2021 Census.
